concept.name: Forward discount
concept.definition: The situation in which a currency's forward exchange rate is below its spot rate, i.e. the currency trades at a discount for future delivery (equivalently, negative forward points for that currency). Under covered interest parity, a currency trades at a forward discount when its interest rate is above that of the other currency in the pair.
concept.intuition: A currency at a forward discount costs less forward than spot — the arithmetic counterpart of its higher interest rate.
concept.mechanics: With the rate quoted as quote currency per base currency, negative forward points (F < S) mean the base currency is at a forward discount and the quote currency at a forward premium. The annualized discount (F - S)/S is tied by covered interest parity to the interest differential, plus any cross-currency basis. High-yielding (carry target) currencies normally trade at a forward discount.
concept.formula: Annualized forward discount = (F - S) / S x (360 / days to maturity) < 0; F = forward rate, S = spot rate.
concept.failure_modes: The discount is not a forecast of depreciation; uncovered interest parity — which would turn the discount into an expected spot change — fails empirically, and high-rate currencies often appreciate instead, which is the basis of the carry trade.
concept.misconceptions: Selling a currency 'because it is at a forward discount' double-counts the interest differential: hedging a high-yielder via forwards surrenders exactly the carry that the discount reflects.
concept.example: If USD/MXN spot is 18.00 and Mexican rates exceed US rates, the 1-year forward might be 19.10: the peso is at a forward discount (it buys fewer dollars forward than spot).

citations.source: BIS Quarterly Review, September 2016 — Covered interest parity lost: understanding the cross-currency basis (Borio, McCauley, McGuire, Sushko)
